2.text: p. 149, Fig. 63, has an amulet like this strung on one of its meshes. Small

3.text: pieces of red cloth or curried leather, roughly fashioned like human figures,

4.text: are often attached to nets, fishing-tackle, rifles, and self-acting bows. They

5.text: represent “assistants,” which were spoken of before.

6.text: FAMILY CHARMS OF THE REINDEER CHUKCHEE. — The family charms are

7.text: more complicated than the individual ones, but we shall see that they consist

8.text: chiefly of amulets of the various kinds described. These amulets are joined

9.text: together and form a sacred object, protecting the material welfare of the

10.text: family, and guarding it against attacks by evil spirits.

11.text: I have mentioned that the family charms of the Reindeer Chukchee

12.text: differ from those of the Maritime people. The family charms and sacred

13.text: things in use among the Reindeer Chukchee protect their material welfare,

14.text: particularly in regard to whatever affects the herd.

15.text: Hearth. — The chief place among the sacred things of the household

16.text: belongs to the hearth itself, to the fire of which a spark is added from each

17.text: of the hereditary fire-tools at every ceremonial. Each family has a fire of

18.text: its own, and interchange of fire is strictly prohibited. Families whose fires

19.text: are derived from different lines of ancestors, even though living for years in

20.text: the same camp, will carefully guard against any contact of their fires. To

21.text: borrow a neighbor’s fire is held to be one of the greatest sins. If a camp

22.text: is pitched on the spot formerly occupied by another family, the Chukchee

23.text: woman, in order to start a new fire, will not avail herself of the coal or

24.text: wood that was left. Even when camped on the treeless tundra, she will

25.text: break up the sledges for fire-wood rather than take a single splinter bearing

26.text: marks of an alien fire. Interchange of household utensils connected with the

27.text: hearth — like kettles, dishes, lamps, receptacles for meat, etc. — is also

28.text: strictly forbidden. It is even considered sinful to warm at one hearth a piece

29.text: of cold meat which has been boiled at another. All these restrictions, how-

30.text: ever, refer only to the “genuine fire,” obtained for a native hearth by means

31.text: of a wooden drill and the sacred fire-board.

32.text: On the other hand, the strike-a-light, sulphur-dish, and matches may be

33.text: freely borrowed and interchanged, because they have nothing to do with the

34.text: sacred family fire. A Chukchee woman will also take from a neighbor of

35.text: her tribe a match, or flint and steel, because these have nothing to do with

36.text: the sacred family fire; but she will not take willow tinder, because it is mixed

37.text: with coal, and the coal was taken from the alien hearth. She will show the

38.text: same aversion to the fire of the Reindeer Koryak, who also have sacred

39.text: fire-tools; but she will not hesitate to borrow a firebrand or burning coals

40.text: from a Russian or from a Lamut.¹

41.text: ¹ I met, however, among the Anui camps, especially In the more remote parts of the country, people who would

42.text: not allow even a match struck in their sleeping-room, fearing contamination of their household penates. No alien man

43.text: would be allowed to busy himself around their fire, not even to put in place a brand or a kettle with food to be cooked.
